Auditing LLM Benchmarks with Item Response Theory

Sander Land Affiliation: Writer, Inc. Email: sander@writer.com    Daniel M. Bikel Affiliation: Writer, Inc. Email: dan.bikel@writer.com
Abstract

LLM benchmark labels are frozen at release and silently copied into downstream benchmarks, errors and all. Our Item Response Theory indicator surfaces these mislabels at 95% precision in the top 200, across 114 models on seven preference and multiple-choice benchmarks, outperforming a supervised classifier. We trace these errors to mechanical labeling rules, upstream errors inherited unchanged from source datasets, and ambiguous items with no defensible single key. The same fit reveals that reward models specialize in stylistic preference over factual knowledge, and exposes one frontier reward model that agrees with detected mislabels at 78% accuracy versus 38% for its peers, consistent with contamination or benchmark-specific over-optimization.
 datasets/Writer/IRT-mislabeled-items

1 Introduction

LLM benchmarks drive model selection, training decisions, and public leaderboards, yet their labels are rarely revisited after release. Once published, labels are effectively frozen and treated as ground truth, even as the models evaluated on them change (Rodriguez et al., 2021; Balepur et al., 2025).

This creates two failure modes that aggregate accuracy hides. First, individual benchmark items can be mislabeled, propagating directly into model rankings and reward-model training data. Because human labeling is expensive, benchmarks are often built from earlier benchmarks or synthetic pipelines, so errors at any stage persist through the chain. Second, individual models can have benchmark-specific performance inconsistent with their behavior elsewhere, ranging from legitimate specialization to contamination or over-optimization.

We address both with Item Response Theory (Hambleton et al., 1991, IRT;), a psychometric framework that jointly estimates latent model abilities and item-level parameters. Our central contribution is a novel mislabel indicator built on the four-parameter logistic (4PL) version of IRT that asks whether an item’s response pattern is better explained by stronger models becoming increasingly correct or increasingly incorrect. The same framework also surfaces anomalies consistent with benchmark contamination or over-optimization, identified through model-level agreement with the items our method flags as mislabels.

This paper contributes: (i) an unsupervised IRT-based annotation-error detector, (ii) an analysis of recurring mislabel patterns across preference and MC benchmarks, and (iii) a model-level diagnostic showing reward-model specialization and anomalous agreement with detected mislabels.

2 Background and Related Work

Item Response Theory (IRT) models the probability that respondent mm gives a correct response to item ii as a parametric function of a latent ability θm\theta_{m} and item-level parameters. The two-parameter logistic form (Birnbaum, 1968) specifies this probability as σ⁡(ai​(θm−bi))\sigma(a_{i}(\theta_{m}-b_{i})), where σ\sigma is the logistic function, aia_{i} is item discrimination, and bib_{i} is item difficulty. The three- and four-parameter extensions (Barton and Lord, 1981) add a lower asymptote cic_{i} to model guessing on multiple-choice items and an upper asymptote did_{i} to model ceiling effects arising from accidental mistakes by high-ability individuals. While the original aim of IRT was to measure human ability, a common use in machine learning has been to measure properties of the items. Prior work has applied IRT to NLP benchmarks to measure dataset quality and construct efficient evaluation subsets (Lalor et al., 2016; Lalor et al., 2018; Rodriguez et al., 2021; Polo et al., 2024), with Vania et al. (2021) showing that IRT reveals structure invisible to aggregate accuracy. More recent work uses IRT to assess reliability and score stability in LLM evaluations (Vendrow et al., 2025; Hofmann et al., 2025) and to drive adaptive testing (Li et al., 2026). These applications largely rely on the 2PL or 3PL parameterization. Rodriguez et al. (2021) use a 4PL upper asymptote as a per-item feasibility score to filter unsolvable items. Our work also applies IRT to study dataset items, at a larger scale than prior efforts and with a forced-ceiling likelihood ratio derived from the upper asymptote as our mislabel indicator. Annotator error detection (AED) has been widely studied in NLP (Klie et al., 2023). Most AED methods score instances using model-internal signals such as training dynamics or prediction uncertainty, often based on an ensemble of trained classifiers, which presupposes a supervised training setup. Label-aggregation methods such as GLAD (Whitehill et al., 2009), which jointly infer annotator ability and item difficulty from a labeling matrix, can also be used for AED. Our setting is post-hoc and model-free at the item level. We score items from a panel of off-the-shelf models’ responses, with no training signal or per-item retraining. Label-error detection has also been studied outside NLP. Northcutt et al. (2021a); Northcutt et al. (2021b) introduce Confident Learning to detect supervised label errors and show that such errors are pervasive in widely-used test sets, with downstream effects on model rankings. Gema et al. (2025) extend this observation to MMLU, demonstrating that label errors in a canonical MC benchmark are substantial enough to shift LLM rankings.

Finally, our error taxonomy connects to work showing that human and LLM preference labels underweight factuality and overvalue surface cues (Hosking et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024). Our model-level anomaly analysis relates to benchmark-contamination work (Shi et al., 2024; Oren et al., 2024).

3 Methods and Results

3.1 Data

We investigate two classes of multiple-choice benchmarks. The first consists of preference benchmarks used to evaluate LLM judges and reward models: RewardBench (pairwise) (Lambert et al., 2025), RewardBench 2 (4-way) (Malik et al., 2026), RM-Bench (pairwise) (Liu et al., 2025b), and JudgeBench (pairwise) (Tan et al., 2025). The second consists of factual 4-way multiple-choice benchmarks: GPQA Diamond (Rein et al., 2024) and MC variants of MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021b) and GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) from Zhang et al. (2024). Most benchmarks include several subsets, such as JudgeBench’s knowledge, reasoning, math, and safety categories. In total this yields 20986 items spanning 32 subsets.

We evaluate 114 models from 2023–2026, including six dedicated reward models. The generative models range from a 0.8B open-weights model to frontier flagships. For generative models, we use a prompt that requests a chosen answer and justification. Non-reasoning models are sampled at temperature 0.30.3 and reasoning models at temperature 0.70.7 to 1.01.0, following models’ recommended defaults. For visualization and evaluation, not for fitting the IRT indicator, we assign each item a weak reference label: label_correct, mislabel, or subjective. We use GPT-5.4 (extra-high) as a consensus aggregator over several strong-model judgments of the reference answer and top alternative. Because GPQA Diamond is expert-authored and difficult to adjudicate without domain expertise, we treat GPQA items as label_correct for these metrics. Prompts for the response models and label aggregator are shown in Appendix F. Subset counts, filter statistics, and gold-label construction are listed in Appendix A.

3.2 4PL IRT model

We fit the four-parameter logistic IRT model (Barton and Lord, 1981).

P⁡(yi​m=1)=ci+(di−ci)​σ​(ai​(θm−bi))P(y_{im}=1)=c_{i}+(d_{i}-c_{i})\,\sigma\!\left(a_{i}(\theta_{m}-b_{i})\right) (1)

Mapping the original psychometric setting onto benchmark evaluation, the respondent becomes model mm with latent labeling ability θm\theta_{m}, and the test item becomes a benchmark item with difficulty bib_{i} and discrimination aia_{i}. The lower asymptote ci∈[0,1]c_{i}\in[0,1] relates to the probability of matching the reference by chance, though it can be lower when a distractor systematically attracts model responses. The upper asymptote di∈[0,1]d_{i}\in[0,1] is the probability that an arbitrarily strong model matches the reference, and is the parameter we exploit for mislabel detection.

IRT models are unidentified up to a joint shift and scale of θ\theta and bb. Adding a constant to all θm\theta_{m} and all bib_{i} leaves the likelihood unchanged, and rescaling both is absorbed into aia_{i}. We resolve this with a method-of-moments anchor:

λ⁡(θ¯ 2+(σ^θ−1)2),λ=10,\lambda\left(\bar{\theta}^{\,2}+(\hat{\sigma}_{\theta}-1)^{2}\right),\qquad\lambda=10,

where θ¯\bar{\theta} and σ^θ\hat{\sigma}_{\theta} are the sample mean and standard deviation of {θm}\{\theta_{m}\}. The penalty pulls the sample mean of θ\theta to zero and its standard deviation to one. All fits minimize the negative log-likelihood of Eq. 1 (plus this anchor) aggregated over observed responses yi​my_{im}, using L-BFGS-B with analytic gradients.

Before fitting, we remove two classes of items that are uninformative for IRT modeling. The tie filter drops 137 items (0.7%) on which the plurality answer among non-reward models was invalid or tied. These concentrate in multi-way RMB-Math and RMB-Code subsets, where multiple options are equivalent or no option is clearly correct. The constant-item filter drops 1685 items (11.1%) on which every generative model gives the same answer. Most constant-filtered items are all-correct; safety subsets account for a large share, reflecting broad model consensus on clear safety cases. The smaller all-wrong population is analyzed separately in Appendix D, since unanimous disagreement with the reference is itself a mislabel signal.

3.3 Parameter estimation

A full per-item 4PL fit involves approximately ∼80,000\sim 80{,}000 parameters, and the loss landscape can contain flat regions and multiple local minima. We therefore use two stages: a constrained preliminary fit that estimates the model ability scale {θm}\{\theta_{m}\} from items aligned with the overall ability ordering, followed by independent per-item fits with model ability held fixed.

Preliminary fit.

We restrict the preliminary fit to items whose correctness pattern agrees with the subset’s overall ability ordering. Specifically, we keep items with ri>0.2r_{i}>0.2, where rir_{i} is the Pearson correlation between the item’s binary correctness vector and each model’s mean accuracy on the remaining items in that subset. This keeps 16300 items. Within this set, we estimate one discrimination as∈[1/15,15]a_{s}\in[1/15,15] per subset rather than per item, bound bi∈[−2,2]b_{i}\in[-2,2] to prevent flat-curve divergence through extreme difficulty values, and fix cic_{i} to the chance floor (12\tfrac{1}{2} or 14\tfrac{1}{4}) and di=1d_{i}=1, yielding a constrained 3PL-style fit. Appendix B reports sensitivity to the rr threshold and the item-level constraint box.

Item-level and forced-ceiling fits.

After the preliminary fit fixes the ability scale, we refit item-level parameters over the full 19164-item fit set with θm\theta_{m} held fixed. Each item is fit independently with ai∈[1/15,15]a_{i}\in[1/15,15], bi∈[−2,2]b_{i}\in[-2,2], and ci,di∈[0,1]c_{i},d_{i}\in[0,1].

When high-ability models systematically miss the reference answer, a 2PL or 3PL fit must absorb the pattern into discrimination or difficulty. The 4PL instead exposes it through the upper asymptote. A low did_{i} means the reference answer remains unlikely even at high ability. This may indicate a mislabeled reference, genuine ambiguity about the best answer, or item difficulty beyond the top models’ ability.

Figure 2 shows this pattern empirically. The joint distribution of bib_{i} and did_{i}, split by weak reference label, places most items near di≈1d_{i}\approx 1, while items labeled mislabel form a low-ceiling population near di≈cid_{i}\approx c_{i}. The separation is along the ceiling dimension rather than difficulty. The fit lowers did_{i} instead of only inflating bib_{i}, which distinguishes unreachable references from merely difficult items.

However, the raw ceiling parameter is nearly bimodal. Of the 19164 items in the fit set, 151 have di<10−3d_{i}<10^{-3} (effectively at the floor) and 12357 have di>0.999d_{i}>0.999 (effectively at the ceiling), leaving little ranking resolution within either mode. We therefore convert the ceiling test into a likelihood-ratio indicator. For each item we independently refit (ai,bi,ci)(a_{i},b_{i},c_{i}) under two forced-ceiling hypotheses, di=1d_{i}=1 and di=0d_{i}=0, and record

Δ​ℓi=ℓi​(di=0)−ℓi​(di=1),\Delta\ell_{i}=\ell_{i}(d_{i}=0)-\ell_{i}(d_{i}=1),

where ℓi​(⋅)\ell_{i}(\cdot) is the optimized average per-respondent log-likelihood for item ii under the specified ceiling. Positive Δ​ℓi\Delta\ell_{i} means the response pattern is better explained by a zero-ceiling fit, i.e. that ability inflates the probability of the non-reference answer. Figure 3 illustrates this contrast. We use this Δ​ℓi\Delta\ell_{i} score as our mislabel indicator.

3.4 Mislabel detection

We compare Δ​ℓi\Delta\ell_{i} against alternative scores derived from the same response matrix, plus plain-IRT and off-the-shelf AED baselines. The unsupervised comparators are raw ceiling (ranking by low did_{i}), preliminary-filter consistency (ranking by low rir_{i}), top-10 disagreement, and overall disagreement. As a supervised comparator, we fit XGBoost on (ai,bi,ci,di)(a_{i},b_{i},c_{i},d_{i}) with five-fold stratified cross-validation.

Table 1 reports performance against the weak reference labels. The forced-ceiling indicator achieves the best AP and P@200 under strict mislabel scoring, and the best AP and precision when subjective items are also treated as positives.

Raw low did_{i} carries much of the signal but loses ranking resolution within its near-bimodal modes. Low rir_{i} and top-10 disagreement are strong near the head of the queue, confirming that high-ability model disagreement is the main empirical signal, but they either require an arbitrary top-kk choice or lack item-level parameters explaining the pattern.

The remaining baselines support the same conclusion. XGBoost trained on the four 4PL parameters does not recover the forced-ceiling contrast. A single-stage 4PL fit and a plain 2PL fit perform well at some head-of-queue cutoffs, but trail on strict P@200 or AP, consistent with ceiling effects being absorbed into raw did_{i}, discrimination, or difficulty.

3.5 Mislabel patterns

Inspecting flagged items by hand (Appendix E) surfaces three recurring sources of label noise (Figure 4).

The most common is construction and verification artifacts. Topic-fit labels, format verifiers, older automatic judges, style-variant templates, and by-construction error injection can all mark a response correct for satisfying the benchmark construction rule rather than for being the better answer. Many of these become letter-vs.-spirit failures. For example, the chosen response satisfies a surface constraint, while the rejected response better satisfies the prompt’s intent. RM-Bench’s style-variant template is a high-volume case. A forced-concise chosen response is paired with a detailed rejected response, so the brevity penalty can outweigh the injected flaw.

A second pattern is source errors inherited unchanged. GSM8K reasoning errors, MMLU-Pro key issues, and original preference-label mistakes reappear in downstream benchmarks, sometimes across many generated variants, after the source label has been treated as settled.

A final group consists of items with no stable single best answer, including duplicate options, convention-dependent answers, and near-equivalent preference pairs. Such examples may be usable as preference-training data, where noise averages over many examples, but are poor benchmark items because each label is treated as ground truth for model ranking. These cases concentrate toward the tail of the ranking and explain much of the precision drop after the highest-ranked items.

3.6 Detecting model-level anomalies

Subset-level ability deviations.

The fitted item parameters enable a separate question: which models show subset-specific departures after their overall level is factored out? We hold (ai,bi,ci,di)(a_{i},b_{i},c_{i},d_{i}) fixed and refit a per-pair ability θm,s\theta_{m,s} for each (model, subset) pair under a Gaussian prior toward the global θm\theta_{m} with precision λθ=0.1\lambda_{\theta}=0.1. We then center within each model, Δ​θm,s=θm,s−θ¯m\Delta\theta_{m,s}=\theta_{m,s}-\bar{\theta}_{m}, where θ¯m\bar{\theta}_{m} is the model’s mean fitted ability across subsets.

Figure 5 shows the resulting structure. Reward models cluster above their own mean on preference benchmarks, especially RewardBench 2 and RM-Bench Safety, and below their mean on factual MC benchmarks such as GSM and MATH. This pattern suggests format-specific specialization, likely amplified by model scale. In particular, reward models appear better calibrated to preference-style comparisons than to factual MC answering. Their average θ¯m\bar{\theta}_{m} therefore understates preference-benchmark performance and overstates factual MC performance. The deviations are consistent but modest, with typical |Δ​θm,s||\Delta\theta_{m,s}| for reward models on preference subsets in the 0.2–0.5 range.

Agreement with detected mislabels.

A sharper anomaly appears when we inspect which models agree with the reference on items flagged as mislabeled. Following Northcutt et al. (2021a), Figure 6 compares accuracy distributions across three slices of the preference and MC item pools, defined either by weak reference labels or by similarly sized slices of the unsupervised indicator (Δ​ℓi<−0.05\Delta\ell_{i}<-0.05, |Δ​ℓi|≤0.05|\Delta\ell_{i}|\leq 0.05, Δ​ℓi>0.05\Delta\ell_{i}>0.05).

On preference benchmarks, most reward models stay within the non-reward distributions and show no systematic tendency to agree with bad references. The exception is Skywork-Reward V2 Llama 8B, a high-scoring reward model on the RewardBench 2 leaderboard. Its agreement with detected mislabels is far outside both its peer group and the non-reward population. The MC panel suggests the effect is preference-specific. On factual MC tasks, reward models neither agree with mislabels at elevated rates nor separate from the non-reward distribution.

Because the effect is concentrated in one reward model, it does not look like a general reward-model tendency to exploit preference-label artifacts. Two mechanisms remain plausible. First, accidental contamination: Skywork-Reward V2 is trained on an unusually large 40M-pair mixture drawn from public preference datasets (Liu et al., 2025a), overlapping the ecosystem from which these benchmarks draw. Second, benchmark-specific over-optimization: public benchmark releases can shape subsequent synthetic preference data and model selection. Response data alone cannot distinguish these mechanisms.

4 Discussion

Both IRT and label-error detection have a rich history in NLP, including some work that touches on both. Our contribution is the specific construction: a forced-ceiling likelihood ratio derived from the 4PL upper asymptote, which we show outperforms the baselines we test. The gain is not that simpler signals fail entirely. Many baselines, including a basic 4PL fit, recover some high-confidence errors. The forced-ceiling score is stronger because it avoids the spurious local minima that can affect a free 4PL fit, and preserves a ranked signal across the full review queue, more clearly highlighting the most suspicious items. Our two-stage pipeline fixes θ\theta before the item refits, so this ratio runs efficiently in parallel, and can be applied post-hoc to new benchmarks.

The practical requirement for applying this mislabel detection pipeline to new benchmarks is modest, requiring only the response matrix with per-item correctness for each model. This is compatible with evaluation aggregators such as Every Eval Ever (Coalition, 2026), which supports both benchmark-level and item-level submissions. Once item-level responses are available for a benchmark, maintainers can rerun the indicator as stronger models arrive, without new inference, and prioritize high-confidence items for review. We deposit our evaluation results, including per-item responses and model justifications, at the Every Eval Ever Datastore11 1 huggingface.co/datasets/evaleval/EEE_datastore. We also release a dataset of detected mislabeled and subjective items on Hugging Face22 2 huggingface.co/datasets/Writer/IRT-mislabeled-items, which includes potential mislabels surfaced by the tie and constant-item filters, our proposed indicator, and our GPT-5.4-based weak reference labels.

The reward-model result also suggests a practical contamination check. Agreement with detected mislabels is not proof of contamination, as a model may share a benchmark’s labeling heuristic for other reasons. However, it is a useful screening signal. Skywork-Reward V2 Llama 8B is the case study here, agreeing with Δ​ℓi\Delta\ell_{i}-flagged references at 78% on preference tasks, far outside peer reward models and the non-reward distribution. When a model agrees unusually often with references that stronger independent models reject, teams should inspect overlap with public benchmark data, synthetic-data recipes, and model-selection criteria before treating leaderboard gains as general progress.

The flagged items also point, after manual review, to preventable failures. Many confirmed errors and ambiguous items come from construction rules that reward proxies for response quality, source labels copied without rechecking, or examples with no stable single best answer. Benchmark builders can reduce these errors by inspecting high-disagreement items before release, validating source labels when converting or augmenting datasets, and avoiding mechanical labeling rules that confuse surface compliance with response quality. After release, the same indicator gets stronger as more diverse models evaluate the benchmark, so newly suspicious items can be prioritized for review rather than silently copied into the next benchmark or training mixture.

5 Limitations

The main limitation of our evaluation is the weak reference labeling procedure. We use GPT-5.4 (extra-high) as a label aggregator over strong-model judgments and model-side justifications, so the labels inherit some limitations of LLM-as-judge evaluation. Exhaustive human adjudication of roughly 20k items is impractical; the weak labels are therefore a scalable proxy for comparing ranking methods and estimating top-of-queue precision, not definitive relabeling of every benchmark item. In human review of the top flagged items (Appendix E), we found that the aggregator accurately detects many failures, but sometimes sides with proponent-model reasoning and endorses the reference where subjective would be more accurate.

The forced-ceiling indicator depends on a panel of models with sufficient ability spread to make θ\theta identifiable. With 114 models spanning 2023–2026, our panel is comfortably above this threshold, but the indicator’s resolution would degrade on benchmarks with fewer high-ability respondents. The per-item refit also assumes the global θ\theta scale generalizes across subsets. Benchmarks built from item distributions very different from those studied here, or dominated by a single model family, may not reproduce the precision numbers we report.

The Skywork-Reward V2 finding is limited by lack of access to its training data and selection procedure. Skywork released training data for an earlier generation of reward models, but not for V2, so we cannot test overlap with the flagged benchmark items directly. High agreement with detected mislabels is therefore a screening signal, not proof of contamination or benchmark-specific over-optimization.

Appendix A Subset statistics

A.1 Model ability scores

Appendix B Preliminary fit and indicator ablations

We check the two fitting choices most likely to affect the forced-ceiling indicator: the item-level constraint box and the preliminary consistency filter used to learn the ability scale.

Constraints on IRT fit.

The default constraints, ai∈[1/15,15]a_{i}\in[1/15,15] and bi∈[−2,2]b_{i}\in[-2,2] with free cic_{i}, are the best bounded setting by strict P@200 and are essentially tied on the mislabel+subjective positive-Δ​ℓi\Delta\ell_{i} set (Figure 7). Relaxing either aia_{i} bound is near-neutral, though removing the lower bound admits the degenerate ai→0a_{i}\to 0 direction. The bib_{i} bounds are asymmetric: removing the lower bound is neutral, while removing the upper bound drops P@200 by around 5%. Fixing cic_{i} to chance results in the largest degradation.

Preliminary rr filter.

Sweeping the preliminary consistency threshold ri>tr_{i}>t from t=0t=0 to 0.80.8 reduces the preliminary set from about 95% of fitted items to about 3%. The default t=0.2t=0.2 improves P@200 from 92% with no pre-filter to 95% while keeping AP near 0.843 (Figure 8). It also excludes 97% of items whose forced-ceiling refit prefers di=0d_{i}=0, while only 30% of excluded items are in that group. Larger thresholds remove more such items but perturb the ranking.

Appendix C GPQA Diamond analysis

GPQA Diamond (expert-authored multiple choice, with both independent expert validators required to answer correctly) is designed as a clean, graduate-level evaluation benchmark. Because the subject matter prevents reliable non-expert adjudication, we treat GPQA items as label_correct for the weak reference metrics in Table 1. This appendix asks the complementary ranking question: how often do held-clean GPQA items appear at the top of the Δ​ℓi\Delta\ell_{i} ranking? GPQA contributes 165 of the 19164 fitted rows (0.86%). By N=200N=200, Δ​ℓi\Delta\ell_{i} surfaces one GPQA item, and by the natural Δ​ℓi>0\Delta\ell_{i}>0 cutoff (N=874N=874{}) it surfaces six (Figure 9). Table 4 lists those six held-clean false positives. The common signature appears to be a transition where weaker models answer near-randomly while stronger models converge on a plausible-looking distractor, exactly the pattern GPQA’s distractors were designed to elicit from non-experts.

Appendix D Filtered Items

D.1 Plurality-tie filtered items

This section samples the 137 items removed by the plurality-tie filter before IRT fitting. Each box header reports the source subset, item count, representative item, and tie count.

D.2 All-wrong filtered items

Table 5 lists the 27 items on which every non-reward generative model in the panel disagreed with the reference answer. These items are dropped by the constant-item filter (Section 3.1) and never enter the IRT fit, but are potential mislabels and we inspect each one by hand. Repeated variants of the same source prompt are collapsed into a single visible row, so the 27 source items fit into 22 rows.

Appendix E Subset mislabel analysis

This section presents selected items among those with forced-ceiling likelihood contrast Δ​ℓi>0.05\Delta\ell_{i}>0.05, excluding GPQA Diamond. All final judgments on these items are human verified.

E.1 GSM-MC (3)

Source: GSM8K final answer with distractors mined from incorrect predictions of ~60 open-source LLMs (Zhang et al., 2024). All issues are inherited from the original GSM8K reference answers.

E.2 MATH-MC: L1–L5 (16)

Source: Hendrycks MATH (L1–L5) with distractors from open-source LLMs. SymPy was used to drop lexically-different-but-semantically-equivalent duplicates (Zhang et al., 2024). Despite this step, every flagged item is a degenerate multiple-choice item where two options encode the same mathematical answer in different surface formats, ‘$’-delimited vs bare LaTeX, percent-suffix duplicates (‘20’ vs ‘20%’), etc.

E.3 RM-Bench (Easy + Normal + Hard) (374)

RM-Bench (Liu et al., 2025b) builds each item from a base preference pair and generates three style variants per side: chosen c0c_{0} concise, c1c_{1} detailed plain text, c2c_{2} markdown; rejected r0/r1/r2r_{0}/r_{1}/r_{2} matching. Difficulty selects the style pair: Easy pairs c2c_{2} with r0r_{0}, Normal pairs c1c_{1} with r1r_{1}, and Hard pairs c0c_{0} with r2r_{2} to test whether reward models prefer style over substance when the underlying preference is fixed.

Three failure modes recur. The c0c_{0} chosen is often condensed past usability, so a detailed rejected with a minor flaw is the better answer rather than evidence of style bias. The synthetic flaw injection sometimes fails, producing content-equivalent pairs. Original-item label errors propagate across all style variants.

E.3.1 RM-Bench: Chat (Easy + Normal + Hard) (151)

Construction: prompts from AlpacaEval; chosen ycy_{c} generated by GPT-4o; rejected yry_{r} created by injecting factual errors into the chosen response via the Many-Shot Jailbreak technique; both manually verified.

E.3.2 RM-Bench: Code (Easy + Normal + Hard) (114)

Construction: HumanEvalPack prompts; GPT-4o generations, with one passing the unit tests labeled chosen and one failing labeled rejected. Flagged items split between incorrect code (where the HumanEvalPack tests miss the specific failure path, so buggy code passes verification and ends up labeled chosen) and subjective formatting differences.

E.3.3 RM-Bench: Math (Easy + Normal + Hard) (56)

Construction: Hendrycks MATH prompts; GPT-4o generations matched against ground-truth, with one match labeled chosen and one mismatch labeled rejected. Flagged items split between factually incorrect references (often across multiple difficulty levels) and subjective formatting differences.

E.3.4 RM-Bench: Safety (Easy + Normal + Hard) (53)

Construction: XSTest, DoNotAnswer, and AI2 Refusal prompts. For benign-but-alarming prompts, chosen is a GPT-4o helpful response and rejected is a GPT-4o over-refusal (over-cautious system prompt); for genuinely harmful prompts, chosen is the GPT-4o refusal and rejected is harmful content from an uncensored Llama-3.1-8B. Flagged items split between confidently incorrect reference answers on prompts with a false premise, and subjective pairs where both responses are low quality.

E.4 JudgeBench

JudgeBench (Tan et al., 2025) pipeline: kk GPT-4o responses sampled per upstream question, labeled by the upstream auto-verifier (regex match) with a GPT-4o-mini re-verifier filtering format-only disagreements; only items with both a correct and an incorrect response are retained.

E.4.1 JudgeBench: Knowledge (6)

All six Knowledge items come from MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024), specifically math, health, other, and psychology. The errors typically trace to MMLU-Pro’s 4-to-10-option augmentation, which uses LLM-generated distractors that can introduce defensible alternative answers or shift the keyed letter away from the actual correct value.

E.4.2 JudgeBench: Reasoning (3)

JudgeBench labels chosen by final-answer match against LiveBench’s expected answer plus a GPT-4o-mini re-verifier. This process can’t distinguish reasoning quality when both responses reach the same number, and forces a pair even when both responses fail with different errors.

E.4.3 JudgeBench: Math (2)

Both items are LiveBench-math problems. JudgeBench labels chosen by LiveBench’s programmatic grader (final boxed answer plus a strict duplicated-letter format check on MC items), which surfaces distinct construction-pipeline issues: format compliance alone can separate responses that reach the same correct numerical answer, and the grader has to pick one convention when the answer hinges on a choice (e.g., real-undefined vs complex extension) so other defensible answers are marked wrong.

E.4.4 JudgeBench: Coding (1)

The single item in this category appears to have been caused by differences in code execution environments.

E.5 RewardBench 1

The original RewardBench (Lambert et al., 2025) consists of several subsets with mainly synthetic labeling strategies.

E.5.1 RewardBench 1: Chat (15)

Notably, every flagged item in our review of RB1 Chat is drawn from AlpacaEval (zero from MT-Bench). AlpacaEval itself ships only prompts and a win-rate metric, not preference pairs; RewardBench synthesizes labels by selecting two AlpacaEval models with a large win-rate gap and labeling the high-win-rate model’s response as chosen and the low-win-rate model’s as rejected, with manual verification of the ranking but no independent rubric over content. This produces a brittle reference signal whenever the high-win-rate model is wrong, off-prompt, or fails an explicit instruction.

E.5.2 RewardBench 1: Chat-Hard (29)

Source: MT-Bench-Hard (chosen 8–7 vs rejected 6–5 on GPT-4-as-judge’s 1–10 scale) and adversarial LLMBar (author-defined: chosen faithfully follows instruction II, rejected deviates from II; filtered to retain items that fool ChatGPT). MT-Bench-Hard is flagged disproportionately (17.8%, 8/45) vs 4.0–6.7% for LLMBar splits. The three boxes below illustrate three distinct construction-rule failures: (i) LLMBar-Neighbor labels chosen by topic-fit alone, so on-topic fabrications inherit the label; (ii) MT-Bench-Hard inherits GPT-4’s verbosity bias, so the longer chosen wins despite a factual reversal; (iii) LLMBar-GPTInst’s instruction-rewrite can accidentally yield two reasonable answers, giving a spurious mislabel signal.

E.5.3 RewardBench 1: Safety (8)

Source: XSTest, Do-Not-Answer, and an in-development AI2 refusals dataset; chosen is a refusal and rejected is harmful/offensive content. All flagged mislabels are over-refusals on plainly benign requests; flagged subjectives are borderline refuse-vs-help calls. One illustrative item below.

E.5.4 RewardBench 1: Reasoning (2)

Source: HumanEvalPack (correct vs buggy code) for the code half, PRM800K (reference vs incorrect model generations) for the math half. Flagged items split between genuine mislabels where the HumanEvalPack unit test misses the failure path of a synthetic bug (so the bug ends up as the gold completion) and false positives where both completions reach the correct answer via different proof styles.

E.6 RewardBench 2

RewardBench 2 (Malik et al., 2026) uses a 1-correct + 3-incorrect 4-completion format rather than RB1’s binary chosen/rejected pair, with each of the five subsets built by a different verification or construction method. Subsubsections below are ordered from fewest to most flagged items in our review.

E.6.1 RewardBench 2: Safety (6)

Construction: CoCoNot-derived prompts with synthetic labels and manual verification. Mislabels either over-refuse a benign request or accept a harmful one inappropriately.

E.6.2 RewardBench 2: Math (7)

Construction: open-ended human math prompts; majority-vote grading to populate 1 correct + 3 incorrect per prompt, then every sample manually verified. Flagged items split between real chosen errors and false positives where a near-duplicate or richer rejected candidate splits the model vote.

E.6.3 RewardBench 2: PreciseIF (8)

Construction: each prompt has an appended IFBench constraint; 1 completion satisfies it and 3 fail, with adherence checked by verifier functions and each example manually verified. The dominant pattern is mechanical-vs-natural compliance: mislabels arise when chosen ticks the constraint literally or hits some sub-clauses but misses others while a rejected weaves the constraint more naturally; the mirror failure also occurs (chosen genuinely satisfies the constraint best but a fluent rejected with weaker compliance wins the model vote).

E.6.4 RewardBench 2: Factuality (20)

Construction: WildChat-derived prompts; chosen are natural gpt-4o completions, rejected are gpt-4o completions generated under a system prompt instructing subtle factual errors; labeled only when two independent LLM judges agree. About half are real factual mislabels (chosen vaguely declines, fabricates, or violates the requested format); the rest split between false positives (chosen correct but a smoother rejected wins the model vote) and subjective trade-offs. Many cases are alt-driven — the actual top-IRT pick is a rejected other than the original.

E.6.5 RewardBench 2: Focus (22)

Construction (LLMBar-style): prompts rewritten by an LM to induce off-topic or unresponsive completions; 1 on-topic completion paired with 3 off-topic ones per item. Flagged items split between real mislabels (chosen has a factual error or under-answers), false positives (chosen on-topic but a stylistically smoother rejected wins the model vote), and subjective trade-offs.

Appendix F Task and Label-Aggregator Prompts

We use two prompt families for our evaluations: task prompts to run the benchmarks themselves, and label-aggregator prompts to assign weak reference labels.

Benchmark Task Prompts. Generative models evaluate preference items using the markdown prompt, and multiple-choice (MC) items using the direct answer-selection prompt, both shown in Table 6. The table displays shortened, formatted examples from real benchmark items; full evaluation runs dynamically substitute each item’s specific conversation, candidates, question, and options. Reward models, conversely, are not prompted with these templates. For preference items, they directly score candidate completions appended to the original conversation; for MC items, they score answer options as assistant responses to the question.

Label-Aggregator Prompts. To evaluate the unsupervised error detector, we use a separate GPT-5.4 label aggregator to label candidate benchmark errors. For each item, the aggregator receives the benchmark content along with up to three high-performing model justifications supporting the reference label, and up to three supporting the strongest alternative. The aggregator is called at temperature 00 with JSON response formatting enabled. The system and user prompts are shown in Table 6.
